items.title: Famine in 1944 affected the grandchildren of survivors
items.claim: The Dutch Hongerwinter (1944-1945) caused severe famine for several months. Decades later, the GRANDchildren of women pregnant during the famine showed altered methylation patterns and different rates of metabolic disease — even though they were never themselves underfed.
items.prompt: How does an environmental stress affect three generations?

options.text: Epigenetic marks (especially DNA methylation patterns) acquired during fetal development can persist into adulthood; some can affect germline cells, allowing the next generation to inherit the modified pattern
It must be a DNA sequence mutation caused by famine
Famine alters social behaviour passed to grandchildren culturally

items.reveal_title: Heijmans, Tobi and colleagues — the Hongerwinter epigenetic study
items.reveal:
Heijmans et al. (2008) compared DNA methylation in adults who had been in utero during the Dutch famine to their unexposed siblings. The famine-exposed showed less methylation at the IGF2 gene 60 years later.

More recent work has shown some methylation marks pass to grandchildren, with associated health correlates.

This is not classical Lamarckism (inheritance of acquired characteristics through soft inheritance). Methylation marks are mostly cleared between generations, but some escape erasure. The mechanisms are still being mapped.

Distinguishing real intergenerational inheritance from confounders (in utero exposure, shared environment) requires careful study design. Animal models (rodents) have been used to confirm causal mechanisms.
items.why: Inheritance is taught as DNA sequence transmission. Some heritable information is encoded above the sequence, in modifications to DNA and chromatin — and famine can leave its mark across decades.

items.title: Bacteria swap genes like trading cards
items.claim: Sexual reproduction is supposedly biology's great innovation for mixing genes. Bacteria don't bother. They share DNA fragments — including whole antibiotic-resistance genes — directly between unrelated species, sometimes across genera.

options.text: Useful mutations spread across the bacterial 'pan-genome' far faster than vertical inheritance allows — antibiotic resistance can jump from one species to another in a single transfer event
Bacteria only share genes within the same species
Horizontal transfer is too rare to matter

items.reveal_title: Three mechanisms keep the bacterial gene pool fluid
items.reveal:
Conjugation: two bacteria form a physical bridge (pilus) and transfer a plasmid.
Transformation: bacteria scoop up loose DNA from the environment.
Transduction: viruses (phages) accidentally package bacterial DNA and inject it into the next host.

The NDM-1 resistance gene, first found in Klebsiella in 2008, jumped via plasmids across at least 11 bacterial species and 4 continents within a decade. Genes encoding beta-lactamases (penicillin breakdown) appear in soil bacteria; clinical pathogens picked them up after antibiotics entered hospitals.

The 'tree of life' for bacteria isn't really a tree — it's a tangled net.
items.why: Evolution is taught as descent with modification along branching lineages. Bacterial evolution is reticular — sideways, not just downward.

items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.
